core.title: Classify each train with its category field
core.given: A planner is authoring or editing a train (a plan artifact defining one planned journey), including its steps, acceptance or outcome
core.when: the train is created, named or renamed, or its scenario semantics change in a way that may alter its category
core.then: Set the train's `category` field to exactly one of nominal, error, alternate or exception, chosen by the category definitions.
prefer: nominal: the intended journey; the domain runs to completion and returns the outcome the job exists to produce.
alternate: another in-domain route to success (input mode, channel, configuration, persona); a success, not a failure.
exception: the domain ran and refused (negative verdict, the business rule working); retry is refused identically (validation, rule violations, policy denials).
error: fault outside the domain; domain never ran, no verdict or postcondition; retry may succeed once the fault clears (crashes, collaborator unavailability, infrastructure).
Reclassify by editing the category field, without a category-driven rename.
avoid: Encoding the category in the train's name or id (category is metadata, not identity).
Labelling a business-rule refusal as error, or an alternate success as a failure.
core.why: Category is metadata, not identity, so a train is reclassified by changing a field rather than its name; the closed set keeps success, in-domain refusal and out-of-domain fault distinct.
evidence: Each train has a `category` field whose value is one of nominal, error, alternate, exception; no other value is used.
The train's name/id does not encode its category, and a reclassification is expressed as a change of the category field without requiring a rename (other unrelated edits in the same change are fine).

Reviewer checks the chosen value against the definitions: did the domain run, did it succeed, is a refusal deterministic on retry; when steps/acceptance change the outcome, the category is re-checked.
verification: Closed-set check: every train definition carries a `category` field whose value is exactly one of nominal, error, alternate, exception; any other value (or a missing field) is a violation. The four value keys are fixed for the taxonomy and are neither renamed nor extended per stack.

Full category definitions govern the choice (used by review and any semantic check): nominal — the intended journey, the domain runs to completion and returns the outcome the job exists to produce; alternate — a different in-domain route to a successful outcome (another input mode, channel, configuration or persona), still a success, not a failure; exception — an in-domain refusal, the domain ran, evaluated the request and rendered a negative verdict, so the refusal is the business rule working and the identical request is refused identically on retry (validation failures, business rule violations, policy denials); error — a fault originating outside the modelled domain, the domain never ran, so no verdict exists and no domain postcondition holds, and the identical request may succeed once the fault clears (crashes, collaborator unavailability, infrastructure faults).

Not covered by mechanical checking: whether the chosen value matches the scenario's semantics (did the domain run, did it succeed, is a refusal deterministic on retry), whether the name/id encodes the category, and whether an outcome-changing edit calls for reclassification — these are semantic, review-level (llm_judged) findings; the mechanical part of the check only enforces the closed set and field presence.

Scope: the check applies to train definitions (the stack's plan artifacts of the train kind) when they are authored or edited; it does not govern the separate family-classification axis or artifacts that do not define trains. Train definitions are located via the profile's plan-artifact kinds; no disposition or suppression is declared by this rule.

values: train category field set or changed
category does not match the scenario's semantics

fires: Planner authors a new train and must set its category.
Planner reclassifies an existing train (e.g. from error to exception).
Planner names or renames a train and might embed its category in the name/id.

Planner edits a train's steps or acceptance so the scenario now ends in a different kind of outcome (e.g. a success path becomes an in-domain refusal or an external fault), which may make the existing category wrong.
doesNotFire: Authoring other plan artifacts (e.g. wagons, WMBTs or docs) that do not define trains.
Classifying a train along the separate family axis (a separate rule governs that axis).
Purely cosmetic edits to a train (typo, formatting) that change neither its outcome semantics, category nor identity.

profileRequirements.meaning: The concrete plan-artifact kinds of the stack, so the core's activation fact file_kind 'train' and the check's scope resolve 'train' to the stack's train-definition artifact kind (in Bun: the train definition files authored by the planner).

bunOnly.text: Term `category` (label 'Test categories'), defined as name -> description: the four values of the train's `category` field. Closed set: nominal, error, alternate, exception; value keys are unchanged from legacy.
bunOnly.reason: The glossary-term registry (term id, display label, name->description shape) is ATDD-Bun sidecar machinery, and 'value keys are unchanged from legacy' is legacy provenance; the core states the same closed set directly in its obligation and verification, without the registry shape.

neutralityNotes: The convention is almost entirely methodology-level: 'train' is a plan-artifact kind of the framework, and `category` with its closed four-value set is framework taxonomy, so the core carries the obligation unchanged and needs no per-stack data beyond the plan-artifact kinds (roles.plan_artifact.kinds). Two things were deliberately neutralized: (1) verifier_detail[0]'s glossary-term registry shape and legacy-parity note are Bun realization details (bunOnly), while the same closed set is enforced in core verification; (2) the doesNotFire reference to the sibling rule id 'planner.train.family' was genericized to 'a separate rule governs that axis', because rule ids belong to the rule set rather than the neutral core. bun.json declares no severity, disposition or suppression, so the core's verification asserts none. Full category definitions are kept verbatim-level in verification[1] so the compressed prefer glosses lose nothing.
